we have developed a method to synchronize music and visual media in real-time, and have demonstrated that this synchronization can be used to support a novel bidirectional human-computer interface.
the score can be a bidirectional user–computer interface that allows for the synchronization of multiple media streams and the representation of a musical performance in terms of the score.
we have designed and implemented an interactive computer system to perform popular music that is based on a score and can adapt to changes in the music.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the representation of popular music scores and their synchronization with performance.
how to represent and manipulate music scores in a computer environment in order to facilitate human–computer performance of popular music.
the design of a system to support the human–computer performance of popular music.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have demonstrated the feasibility of a computer-based system that can support a wide variety of popular music, including jazz, blues, and rock, with a score representation and synchronization approach that is robust and flexible.
the score is a very powerful representation for popular music, but that it needs to be extended to include more information, and that the score itself needs to be made dynamic and interactive.
the score is the most important element of the system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed an approach to the representation of music that is flexible enough to be used as an interface to a computer system for performance, while at the same time being expressive enough for use by humans as a score.
we are developing an active score, which is both a representation of a performance and an interface that can be used for performance.
it is possible to create an active score that can be used for both representation and synchronization in human–computer performance of popular music.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a score can be used to synchronize human and computer performers, even when the computer is performing in real time, with a latency of 10 to 20 ms, and even when the score is not fixed, but may be rearranged or even “flattened” during performance.
it is possible to represent the score in a way that is both expressive and computationally tractable, and to use this representation to synchronize human and computer performance of popular music.
a digital score can be a useful interface for both human and computer performers, and that a computer can provide a useful interface to a human performer.
